screens.title: Decentralized Storage & IPFS
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll connect practical architecture decisions with the decentralized storage tools you'll use in real DApps. Blockchains are brilliant for small, critical state: ownership, signatures, and transactional records. They are not designed for megabytes of images or video. You'll learn why storing large files on-chain is costly and slow, how content addressing makes integrity simple, and how IPFS implements content-addressed storage with cryptographic identifiers called CIDs. We'll also show the standard developer flow: add file to IPFS, receive a CID, and store that CID on-chain so your smart contract points to immutable off-chain content. By the end you'll see concrete commands and code you can reuse in a DApp, and you'll understand practical caveats like pinning, privacy, and gateway reliance. This matters because designing storage correctly keeps gas costs low, preserves network performance, and gives users durable, censorship-resistant access to their assets. Think of this lesson as a toolbox: small on-chain proofs and large off-chain content linked by a hash. How will you use CIDs in your next smart contract design?

screens.title: Why blockchains are ill-suited for large files
screens.narratorSegment: Blockchains replicate state across many nodes to achieve consensus and immutability. That replication is why blockchains excel at small, critical records but fail when asked to store megabytes of arbitrary files. Each added byte is duplicated across the entire network and must be agreed upon by consensus, which increases storage costs and transaction fees. A concrete example: storing a 10 megabyte video on a typical smart-contract platform would multiply that 10 megabytes by the number of full nodes, and the gas required to write such data would make the operation prohibitively expensive. The right architectural pattern is to store a tiny, verifiable token on-chain — a cryptographic hash — and keep the heavy payload off-chain on a decentralized storage network. A common misconception is to assume that immutability equals on-chain storage; instead immutability can be achieved by storing a content hash on-chain and the content itself off-chain. Takeaway: prefer proofs on-chain and payloads off-chain. How would you explain that trade-off to a product owner who wants all data on-chain? Why blockchains are ill-suited for large files means blockchains are optimized for small, immutable state. large files should be stored off-chain with on-chain hashes serving as immutable pointers.. In practical terms, replication, consensus, and gas costs make on-chain file storage impractical. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Blockchains replicate every byte of stored state across many nodes. This gives immutability and censorship resistance but makes bulky storage expensive and slow.
Example: 10MB video

On-chain
  • Transactions and small proofs

Off-chain
  • Large files, media, datasets
  • Distributed hosts like IPFS
Analogy
Think of the blockchain as a ledger of receipts: each receipt can reference a file stored in a warehouse. The ledger keeps proof of the file, not the file itself.

screens.title: Content addressing vs Location addressing
screens.narratorSegment: Content addressing and location addressing are two fundamentally different ways to identify files. Location addressing answers 'where is the file' by naming a server or path — for example a typical web URL that points to a specific host. That approach depends on that host being available and honest. Content addressing asks 'what is the file' and uses a cryptographic hash of the file's bytes as the identifier. This ensures integrity: if the file changes, the hash changes. A concrete example: two servers can host the same image, but only content addressing can verify that the bytes are identical because the CID will match. A common misconception is that content addressing requires central coordination; it does not. The CID is derived from the data itself. This distinction matters for DApps because storing the CID on-chain gives you an immutable proof of the exact file content without trusting any particular host. Ask yourself: would you rather reference a server you must trust, or a cryptographic fingerprint you can verify? Content addressing vs Location addressing means location points to where content lives; content addressing names the content itself so integrity is verifiable and decentralized.. In practical terms, why asking 'what is this file?' is stronger than 'where is this file?'. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Content vs Location
Location addressing (HTTP)
A URL points to a specific server and path. If the server moves or the file is replaced, the URL no longer guarantees the original content.
  • Depends on server availability
  • Can be modified without notice
Content addressing (IPFS)
A CID is a cryptographic hash of the content. Any change results in a different CID, so the identifier guarantees integrity.
  • Host-agnostic retrieval
  • Immutable content identity
Concrete example
Two websites can serve an image named "logo.png". Only a CID proves that both deliver the same bytes. If you store the CID on-chain, anyone can fetch from any IPFS node and validate the content is unchanged.
Misconception check
Content addressing does not remove the need to host content; it only makes the identity verifiable. You still need nodes to serve the bytes.
Key takeaway
CIDs prove exactly what you requested, independent of where it is hosted.

screens.title: IPFS architecture and core principles
screens.narratorSegment: IPFS is a peer-to-peer distributed file system that identifies content by its cryptographic hash. When you add a file, IPFS breaks it into chunks, hashes each chunk, and stores a Merkle-style DAG that links chunks and metadata. The resulting Content Identifier, or CID, is derived from that structure and uniquely identifies the file. Retrieving a CID causes the network to find nodes that host the required chunks and reassemble them. A practical example: adding a 1 megabyte image will produce several chunk hashes and a root CID. If any chunk changes, the root CID changes, preserving integrity. A common misconception is that IPFS is a single centralized server; it is not. It is a network of nodes that can each serve chunks, and availability comes from how many nodes pin or host the content. In production you should plan for persistence by pinning and consider using multiple gateways or pinning services for redundancy. The core insight: IPFS separates identity from location and builds a content-linked DAG to ensure verifiable, distributed storage. IPFS architecture and core principles means ipfs creates a content-linked dag of hashed chunks; the cid names that dag and ensures integrity and reconstructability.. In practical terms, chunking, hashing, and content addressing at a glance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: IPFS creates a content-linked DAG of hashed chunks; the CID names that DAG and ensures integrity and reconstructability.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › IPFS architecture
How files are stored
  1. File is split into chunks.
  2. Each chunk is hashed and linked in a Merkle-like DAG.
  3. A root CID identifies the entire structure.
Resilience
Multiple nodes can host chunks. If one node goes offline, others can serve the same chunks to reassemble the file.
Misconception
IPFS does not automatically keep your file available forever; adding is not equivalent to pinning for persistence.
Visualized block map
Chunks
Many small hashed pieces
Merkle DAG
Links chunks to a root CID for integrity
CID
Cryptographic identifier of the DAG
Retrieval
Network finds nodes hosting chunks and reassembles file
Key takeaway
IPFS builds verifiable content structures: chunk, hash, link, identify with a CID that guarantees integrity.

screens.title: How IPFS adds and retrieves files
screens.narratorSegment: The IPFS add and retrieve flow is straightforward and repeatable. First, start an IPFS daemon so your node participates in the network. Next, add a file using the ipfs add command. IPFS responds with an added line that includes a CID — this is your content-addressed identifier. To read the file, use ipfs cat with the CID or open it via a public gateway URL. A concrete example: create hello. txt with the text "Hello Cohortia!" and run ipfs add hello. txt; you will receive a CID string beginning with a content prefix. Use ipfs cat and that CID to see the original text. A common misconception is that adding a file immediately makes it globally persistent; in reality, only your node hosts it until others pin or replicate it. The practical step after adding is to pin the CID to ensure persistence, or use a pinning service. Final takeaway: the add→CID→store-on-chain→retrieve loop is the pattern you will reuse in NFTs and DApps that need verifiable off-chain assets. How IPFS adds and retrieves files means add file to ipfs → receive cid → optionally pin for persistence → store cid on-chain → retrieve by cid when needed.. In practical terms, step-by-step developer flow for file lifecycle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › IPFS add & retrieve
Steps
  1. Start IPFS daemon: ipfs daemon
  2. Add file: ipfs add filename
  3. Get CID from response and use ipfs cat CID to view
  4. Optional: pin CID or use pinning service
Concrete example
Create hello.txt with "Hello Cohortia!", run ipfs add hello.txt, note the returned CID, then ipfs cat that CID to see the content.
Key takeaway
The CID is your verifiable pointer. Pin it for availability and store it on-chain when you need an immutable reference.
CLI example
# Start the daemon
ipfs daemon

# Add a file
ipfs add hello.txt
# output: added Qm... hello.txt

# Read file
ipfs cat Qm...
Pro tip
After adding, immediately pin the CID on a remote pinning service or additional nodes if you need long-term availability.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › ipfs-http-client example
Setup
Install ipfs-http-client in your Node or frontend project and ensure an IPFS daemon or remote gateway with HTTP API is available.
Use case
Upload a user's NFT image, get the CID, include it in an NFT metadata JSON, then store the metadata CID on-chain.
Misconception
Do not assume public gateways are always available during testing; use a local daemon for development when possible.
Code snippet
import { create } from 'ipfs-http-client';

// Connect to a local IPFS node
const ipfs = create({ host: 'localhost', port: 5001, protocol: 'http' });

async function uploadFileToIPFS(fileContent) {
  try {
    const { cid } = await ipfs.add(fileContent);
    console.log("Uploaded to IPFS. CID:", cid.toString());
    return cid.toString();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error uploading to IPFS:", error);
    return null;
  }
}

async function retrieveFileFromIPFS(cid) {
  try {
    const chunks = [];
    for await (const chunk of ipfs.cat(cid)) {
      chunks.push(chunk);
    }
    const fileContent = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString();
    console.log("Retrieved from IPFS:", fileContent);
    return fileContent;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error retrieving from IPFS:", error);
    return null;
  }
}
Example flow
Read file into ArrayBuffer, pass to uploadFileToIPFS, receive CID string, then send CID to your smart contract as a metadata pointer.

screens.title: Smart contracts storing IPFS CIDs
screens.narratorSegment: A standard pattern in NFT contracts is to store a token's metadata URI as a string that contains an IPFS CID or ipfs scheme. The blockchain stores an immutable pointer — the CID — while the heavy metadata and image data remain off-chain. The example Solidity snippet in the chapter uses a mapping from token ID to string, a setter function that saves the token's URI, and a public accessor to retrieve it. A concrete scenario: when minting, the frontend uploads the image and metadata to IPFS, receives a metadata CID, then calls setTokenURI with the tokenId and that CID to link the token. A common mistake is embedding the full file bytes on-chain or assuming the CID will not change; in fact, a new version requires a new CID, so mutable content should use name systems if needed. Final takeaway: store the CID on-chain as a small, verifiable reference, and design your minting flow so the frontend uploads first and the contract stores the resulting CID. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Store CIDs on-chain
Pattern
Upload asset and metadata to IPFS, get metadata CID, then call a contract function to persist that CID against a token ID or record.
Practical note
Ensure that the frontend uploads and pins content before calling the smart contract so the CID remains available after minting.
Key takeaway
Store only the CID on-chain. The CID guarantees integrity without the storage cost of the payload.
Solidity example
// Example: NFT contract storing IPFS CID
contract MyNFT {
    mapping(uint256 => string) private _tokenURIs; // Maps token ID to IPFS CID

    function setTokenURI(uint256 tokenId, string memory tokenURI) public {
        // Only owner or authorized can set URI
        _tokenURIs[tokenId] = tokenURI;
    }

    function tokenURI(uint256 tokenId) public view returns (string memory) {
        return _tokenURIs[tokenId];
    }
}
Example flow
Frontend uploads image and metadata to IPFS, gets metadata CID, then calls setTokenURI(tokenId, metadataCID) so the token points to the IPFS metadata.

screens.title: Pinning and persistence
screens.narratorSegment: Pinning is the practice of instructing an IPFS node to retain a piece of content so it won't be removed by garbage collection. When you ipfs add a file, it typically lives on your local node. If your node goes offline and no other node has pinned the content, the file may become unavailable. Pinning services or additional nodes are used to ensure persistence. A concrete example is uploading an NFT image and then pinning it via a service or multiple nodes so collectors can always access it by CID. A common mistake is to assume that adding once is enough; without pinning or replication, availability is fragile. Another practical point is that pinning does not change the CID: it simply ensures the bytes remain hosted by chosen nodes. Final takeaway: for production-grade availability, include pinning, replication, or a commercial pinning service in your deployment plan. Pinning and persistence means pinning keeps content hosted on chosen nodes to prevent garbage collection and ensure long-term availability of cids.. In practical terms, making content available over time in a distributed network. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Pinning & Persistence
What pinning does
Pinning marks content to be retained on a node and prevents it from being garbage collected during cleanup. It guarantees a node will continue to serve the content.
Example
After uploading NFT metadata, pin the CID on at least one reliable node or use a pinning service to avoid availability loss.
Common mistake
Assuming public gateways will always have your content. Gateways are convenient but not a guarantee of long-term hosting.
Persistence options
  • Run your own IPFS node and pin the content
  • Use a pinning service or multiple nodes for redundancy
  • Replicate content across trusted hosts
Key takeaway
Pinning is essential for production availability. Plan replication and pinning as part of your deployment checklist.

screens.title: Privacy, mutability, and gateway reliance
screens.narratorSegment: IPFS defaults to public content: any node with the CID can request the data. That means you should not post sensitive private information to IPFS unless it is encrypted. For mutable data, IPFS's content addressing produces a new CID for each change; that is a feature for integrity but a hurdle for mutable content. Systems such as IPNS or other naming systems provide mutable pointers to CIDs, but they add complexity. Gateways let web browsers access IPFS via HTTP, which is convenient for users, but relying solely on a public gateway recreates a single point of failure. A concrete example: a DApp that stores private user profile data on IPFS without encryption exposes that data to anyone with the CID or who can guess it. A common misconception is that IPFS provides confidentiality; it provides integrity and availability, not privacy. Final takeaway: design for privacy and mutability explicitly — encrypt private content and use name systems or application-level pointers for mutable resources, and do not assume gateways will always be available. Privacy, mutability, and gateway reliance means ipfs provides integrity and distribution, not automatic privacy or mutability; plan encryption, naming, and redundancy accordingly.. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Privacy & Gateways
Privacy
Do not store unencrypted sensitive data on IPFS. Anyone who can access a CID can request the content if it is hosted.
Mutability
Every content change yields a new CID. Use name systems if you need a stable mutable pointer to the latest CID.
Misconception
IPFS is not confidential by default. Integrity is guaranteed by CIDs, privacy is the developer's responsibility.
Gateway reliance
A public gateway provides HTTP access to IPFS content but introduces a single point you may rely on. For resilience, encourage running nodes or use multiple gateways.
Key takeaway
Design for privacy, mutability, and redundancy up front. Encryption and pinning are core operational requirements.

screens.title: Activity: Upload NFT metadata to IPFS
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through uploading an NFT metadata JSON to IPFS and retrieving its CID. Start by ensuring your IPFS daemon is running. Create a file named nft_metadata. json with fields like name, description, and image containing an ipfs:// path to an image CID. Run ipfs add nft_metadata. json and copy the returned CID. Open a gateway URL with that CID to verify the JSON displays. A practical tip: upload your image first, note its CID, then reference that CID in the image field of your metadata before adding the metadata file. A frequent mistake is uploading metadata that references an image that was never uploaded or pinned. After obtaining the metadata CID, consider pinning both image and metadata CIDs. Steps

screens.title: Operational best practices for decentralized storage
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting decentralized storage in production, follow a short operational checklist. First, always upload and verify assets before writing their CID on-chain. This prevents dangling pointers. Second, pin critical content on at least one reliable node and consider a commercial pinning service for durability. Third, plan for privacy: encrypt any sensitive payloads before uploading to IPFS so only authorized clients can decrypt them. Fourth, avoid single gateway reliance by supporting multiple gateways or encouraging users to run a node. Fifth, for mutable content decide whether to store an updating pointer like IPNS or to accept immutable versions with new CIDs. A concrete example: in an NFT mint flow, upload image and metadata, pin both, then call the mint function with the metadata CID. A frequent mistake is trusting a single gateway or failing to pin media referenced in metadata. Final takeaway: treat IPFS like part of your infrastructure stack — test uploads, pin for persistence, encrypt where necessary, and document the recovery process. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll connect practical architecture decisions with the decentralized storage tools you'll use in real DApps. Blockchains are brilliant for small, critical state: ownership, signatures, and transactional records. They are not designed for megabytes of images or video. You'll learn why storing large files on-chain is costly and slow, how content addressing makes integrity simple, and how IPFS implements content-addressed storage with cryptographic identifiers called CIDs. We'll also show the standard developer flow: add file to IPFS, receive a CID, and store that CID on-chain so your smart contract points to immutable off-chain content. By the end you'll see concrete commands and code you can reuse in a DApp, and you'll understand practical caveats like pinning, privacy, and gateway reliance. This matters because designing storage correctly keeps gas costs low, preserves network performance, and gives users durable, censorship-resistant access to their assets. Think of this lesson as a toolbox: small on-chain proofs and large off-chain content linked by a hash. How will you use CIDs in your next smart contract design?

These objectives map the practical skills you will practice. First, you will explain why storing large files directly on a blockchain is inefficient and costly. That means you can describe the replication and gas-cost implications that make megabyte-scale storage impractical. Second, you will understand content addressing: how cryptographic hashes identify content instead of a server location, and why a single-bit change produces a new identifier. Third, you will describe IPFS architecture and its core principles, such as chunking, hashing, and distributed retrieval. Fourth, you will demonstrate adding and retrieving files using command-line tools so you can prove the flow works on your machine. Each objective includes a competency milestone that ties a hands-on action to a verification step. Practically, these skills ensure you can design a DApp that keeps on-chain state small and verifiable while relying on a resilient off-chain storage layer. Consider how each objective will reduce your gas bills and increase your data durability in production.

These additional objectives focus on putting IPFS into production workflows. First, you will integrate IPFS content hashes into smart contracts so a token or record can point to immutable metadata stored off-chain. Second, you will learn about pinning and persistence: adding content to IPFS is not the same as guaranteeing it remains hosted, so you'll learn services and techniques to pin content. Third, you'll practice privacy and mutability trade-offs: IPFS content is public by default, and mutable data must be handled with alternate systems or pointers. Fourth, you'll complete a hands-on activity: upload NFT metadata JSON to IPFS, retrieve its CID, and reflect on how to link it to a token ID in Solidity. Each objective strengthens your ability to build resilient, efficient DApps that separate proofs from payloads and make robust design decisions about storage and availability.

Blockchains replicate state across many nodes to achieve consensus and immutability. That replication is why blockchains excel at small, critical records but fail when asked to store megabytes of arbitrary files. Each added byte is duplicated across the entire network and must be agreed upon by consensus, which increases storage costs and transaction fees. A concrete example: storing a 10 megabyte video on a typical smart-contract platform would multiply that 10 megabytes by the number of full nodes, and the gas required to write such data would make the operation prohibitively expensive. The right architectural pattern is to store a tiny, verifiable token on-chain — a cryptographic hash — and keep the heavy payload off-chain on a decentralized storage network. A common misconception is to assume that immutability equals on-chain storage; instead immutability can be achieved by storing a content hash on-chain and the content itself off-chain. Takeaway: prefer proofs on-chain and payloads off-chain. How would you explain that trade-off to a product owner who wants all data on-chain? Why blockchains are ill-suited for large files means blockchains are optimized for small, immutable state. large files should be stored off-chain with on-chain hashes serving as immutable pointers.. In practical terms, replication, consensus, and gas costs make on-chain file storage impractical. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Content addressing and location addressing are two fundamentally different ways to identify files. Location addressing answers 'where is the file' by naming a server or path — for example a typical web URL that points to a specific host. That approach depends on that host being available and honest. Content addressing asks 'what is the file' and uses a cryptographic hash of the file's bytes as the identifier. This ensures integrity: if the file changes, the hash changes. A concrete example: two servers can host the same image, but only content addressing can verify that the bytes are identical because the CID will match. A common misconception is that content addressing requires central coordination; it does not. The CID is derived from the data itself. This distinction matters for DApps because storing the CID on-chain gives you an immutable proof of the exact file content without trusting any particular host. Ask yourself: would you rather reference a server you must trust, or a cryptographic fingerprint you can verify? Content addressing vs Location addressing means location points to where content lives; content addressing names the content itself so integrity is verifiable and decentralized.. In practical terms, why asking 'what is this file?' is stronger than 'where is this file?'. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IPFS is a peer-to-peer distributed file system that identifies content by its cryptographic hash. When you add a file, IPFS breaks it into chunks, hashes each chunk, and stores a Merkle-style DAG that links chunks and metadata. The resulting Content Identifier, or CID, is derived from that structure and uniquely identifies the file. Retrieving a CID causes the network to find nodes that host the required chunks and reassemble them. A practical example: adding a 1 megabyte image will produce several chunk hashes and a root CID. If any chunk changes, the root CID changes, preserving integrity. A common misconception is that IPFS is a single centralized server; it is not. It is a network of nodes that can each serve chunks, and availability comes from how many nodes pin or host the content. In production you should plan for persistence by pinning and consider using multiple gateways or pinning services for redundancy. The core insight: IPFS separates identity from location and builds a content-linked DAG to ensure verifiable, distributed storage. IPFS architecture and core principles means ipfs creates a content-linked dag of hashed chunks; the cid names that dag and ensures integrity and reconstructability.. In practical terms, chunking, hashing, and content addressing at a glance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The IPFS add and retrieve flow is straightforward and repeatable. First, start an IPFS daemon so your node participates in the network. Next, add a file using the ipfs add command. Pinning is the practice of instructing an IPFS node to retain a piece of content so it won't be removed by garbage collection. When you ipfs add a file, it typically lives on your local node. If your node goes offline and no other node has pinned the content, the file may become unavailable. Pinning services or additional nodes are used to ensure persistence. A concrete example is uploading an NFT image and then pinning it via a service or multiple nodes so collectors can always access it by CID. A common mistake is to assume that adding once is enough; without pinning or replication, availability is fragile. Another practical point is that pinning does not change the CID: it simply ensures the bytes remain hosted by chosen nodes. IPFS defaults to public content: any node with the CID can request the data. That means you should not post sensitive private information to IPFS unless it is encrypted. For mutable data, IPFS's content addressing produces a new CID for each change; that is a feature for integrity but a hurdle for mutable content. Systems such as IPNS or other naming systems provide mutable pointers to CIDs, but they add complexity. Gateways let web browsers access IPFS via HTTP, which is convenient for users, but relying solely on a public gateway recreates a single point of failure. A concrete example: a DApp that stores private user profile data on IPFS without encryption exposes that data to anyone with the CID or who can guess it. A common misconception is that IPFS provides confidentiality; it provides integrity and availability, not privacy. When adopting decentralized storage in production, follow a short operational checklist. First, always upload and verify assets before writing their CID on-chain. This prevents dangling pointers. Second, pin critical content on at least one reliable node and consider a commercial pinning service for durability. Third, plan for privacy: encrypt any sensitive payloads before uploading to IPFS so only authorized clients can decrypt them. Fourth, avoid single gateway reliance by supporting multiple gateways or encouraging users to run a node. Fifth, for mutable content decide whether to store an updating pointer like IPNS or to accept immutable versions with new CIDs. A concrete example: in an NFT mint flow, upload image and metadata, pin both, then call the mint function with the metadata CID. A frequent mistake is trusting a single gateway or failing to pin media referenced in metadata. Final takeaway: treat IPFS like part of your infrastructure stack — test uploads, pin for persistence, encrypt where necessary, and document the recovery process. Let's recap three key concepts to take forward. First, decentralized storage separates proofs from payloads: keep small, verifiable hashes on-chain and large files off-chain to save cost and preserve performance. Second, content addressing via CIDs provides integrity: the CID is a cryptographic fingerprint of the content, and any change creates a new CID. Third, pinning and operational discipline ensure availability: without pinning, added files may disappear when nodes go offline. As you design DApps, these three ideas guide your storage architecture and operational decisions. Three compact definitions to keep handy. Decentralized Storage: a peer-to-peer distribution of data that reduces single points of failure and offers censorship resistance. IPFS: an implementation that uses chunking and content-addressed Merkle DAGs to identify and retrieve content by CID. Content Identifier (CID): the cryptographic hash that names the content; if the content changes, the CID changes.
